p: This bill is a symbolic pro forma measure introduced before the Throne Speech
It asserts the Legislative Assembly's right to sit and act without Crown permission
It affirms lawmakers can give priority to matters other than those raised by the Sovereign
The practice traces back to at least 1558 and was codified by the House of Commons in 1604
It follows a tradition used in certain other parliamentary jurisdictions to mark the first bill's constitutional importance
Declares the last Friday of June each year as Buy Ontario, Buy Canadian Day
Lets the LCBO be directed to set up a system for direct manufacturer-to-consumer liquor sales across provinces
Allows the Minister of Finance to sign interprovincial deals enabling cross-border liquor sales to consumers
Creates a new law letting Ontario recognize goods and service authorizations from other provinces as equivalent to Ontario's
Sets deadlines for Ontario bodies to certify workers already certified in another province, including a 30-day decision limit
Grants a one-time six-month temporary certification for out-of-province certified workers applying in Ontario
Creates a fine up to $25,000 (first offence) or $50,000 (repeat) for false claims to get this temporary certification
Amends the Gift of Life Act to allow public identification of deceased organ or tissue donors
Only the deceased person's name may be used, no other identifying details or transplant date disclosed
Identification must be for memorial or appreciation purposes as the hospital sees fit
At least six months must have passed since the transplant before public identification
Consent for public identification must be obtained from the person who gave or would give substitute consent
The short title of the Act is the Robbie's Legacy Act (Honouring Beloved Organ and Tissue Donors), 2025
Comes into force on the day it receives Royal Assent
Changes organ and tissue donation from opt-in consent to a presumed consent (opt-out) system after death
People 16 or older can object to tissue removal before death, in writing, orally with witnesses, or by recorded message
Parents or guardians must consent on behalf of children under 16 before tissue can be removed after death
Family members, in a set order (spouse, children, parents, siblings, next of kin), can object on behalf of someone who died without objecting
Hospitals and other designated facilities must notify Ontario Health when a patient dies or death is imminent
Ontario Health must create and maintain a registry recording people's objections or consents to tissue removal
Ontario Health's role expands to plan, coordinate and support tissue removal, donation and transplant activities
Restricts electricity and gas companies (IESO, Ontario Power Generation, gas utilities) from procuring goods or services based on their country or region of origin, as set by regulation.
Blocks lawsuits or compensation claims against government and energy bodies related to these new procurement restrictions.
Replaces the Endangered Species Act with a new Species Conservation Act, changing how species are listed, protected and permitted.
Removes mandatory listing of at-risk species and makes government response statements and management plans optional or repealed.
Winds up the existing Endangered Species Act agency and transfers its funds to a new Species Conservation Account controlled by the Crown.
Allows the Minister to cancel mining claims, leases or licences if doing so protects the 'strategic national mineral supply chain'.
Creates Special Economic Zones where trusted projects can be exempted from provincial laws, regulations and municipal by-laws.
Bans consuming an illegal substance in a public place, with exemptions such as supervised consumption sites
Allows police or provincial offences officers to order people to stop consuming, leave the area, or provide identification
Lets officers seize, remove and destroy substances believed to be illegal, and send samples for analysis
Allows arrest without warrant for offences under this new Act
Sets penalties of up to $10,000 fine or six months imprisonment, or both, for breaking these rules
Protects people seeking emergency help from being charged based on evidence from that call
Adds trespassing aggravating factors, like ignoring a 24-hour notice to leave or being likely to trespass again
Requires health professionals to treat patients with fairness, not just sensitivity and respect
Makes charging patients an unfair fee for a service a form of professional misconduct
Allows discipline panels to order reimbursement of unfair fees and a three-month licence suspension
Requires Colleges' patient relations programs to include measures preventing unfair fees
Lets Council make regulations defining what counts as an 'unfair fee'
Allows the Director to revoke or suspend a health centre's licence for charging unfair fees
Restricts eliminating licensed services unless linked to unfair fee concerns
Amends the Workplace Safety and Insurance Act, 1997 to reclassify certain employers
Employers operating residential care facilities become Schedule 1 employers under the Act
This includes retirement homes, rest homes and senior citizens' residences
Employers operating group homes are also made Schedule 1 employers
Applies to both public and private employers in these industries
The Act takes effect six months after receiving Royal Assent
Short title is the WSIB Coverage for Workers in Residential Care Facilities and Group Homes Act, 2025
Lets the provincial cabinet, instead of cities, set a code of conduct for city and municipal councillors and local board members
Gives Ontario's Integrity Commissioner new duties, including training local integrity commissioners and reviewing conflict of interest concerns
Allows a local integrity commissioner to recommend removing a councillor's seat after finding a serious code violation causing harm to someone
Requires Ontario's Integrity Commissioner to independently investigate before a council seat can be declared vacant
Requires council to vote within 30 days on a removal recommendation, with near-unanimous support needed to approve it
A councillor removed this way is barred from council or local board seats for four years
Bars starting or finishing these removal inquiries during election nomination and voting periods
Requires bail sureties, and former sureties who owe money to the Crown, to provide information as set out in regulations
Lets more people apply for restraining orders on behalf of someone who fears for their safety, with court or regulatory approval
Makes voyeurism a registrable sex offence under Christopher's Law regardless of any separate court order
Lets police chiefs request temporary policing help from agencies in other Canadian provinces, not just First Nation police
Lets the Inspector General impose interim measures like suspension on police board members while investigating a Minister's complaint
Requires new provincial judges to promise not to seek a transfer for five years, and reworks the judicial candidate recommendation process
Creates a new law letting landlords be fined or jailed for knowingly allowing drug production or trafficking on their property
Creates a separate board of health for the City of Hamilton, appointed entirely by the city, replacing the city's direct role
Applies French Language Services Act rules to the Connecting Care Act's Service Organization
Creates a new law requiring health care staffing agencies to report billing, pay rate and administrative data to the Minister every six months
Sets fines up to $10,000 for individuals and $25,000 for corporations that breach the new staffing agency reporting law
Requires local medical officers of health to get written approval from the Chief Medical Officer of Health before issuing class orders
Allows nurse practitioners, not just physicians, to perform blood testing duties under the Mandatory Blood Testing Act
Lets a new 'prescribed organization' create digital health identifiers and manage related personal health information, with privacy and breach-notification rules
Increases the Ontario small business deduction rate from 8.3 per cent to 9.9 per cent
Raises the business limit for the small business deduction from $500,000 to $600,000
Adjusts the surtax formula for Ontario small businesses to match the new $600,000 limit
Changes take effect on January 1, 2026
Also known as the Cutting Taxes on Small Businesses Act, 2025
Creates the Primary Care Act, 2025, setting Ontario's vision for publicly funded primary care
Sets six objectives: province-wide access, connected services, convenient timing, inclusive and non-discriminatory care, empowered access to personal health information, and responsive system
Requires the Minister to publish an annual report on progress toward these objectives, starting within one year of the Act coming into force
Report must include the percentage of insured persons with an ongoing relationship with a primary care clinician or team
Clarifies the Act creates no private legal right, duty of care, or fiduciary duty for any person
States that failing to comply with the Act does not invalidate any related policy, law, regulation or decision
Allows the Lieutenant Governor in Council to make regulations detailing objectives, reporting information and how reports are published
Requires long-term care homes to have organized dementia care programs and cultural, linguistic, religious and spiritual support programs
Creates new offences for abuse or neglect of residents by licensees, staff, volunteers and service providers
Makes licensees guilty of an offence for any failure to comply with the Act or regulations
Replaces the Medical Director role with a Clinical Director, who may be a physician or extended-class registered nurse
Gives inspectors and provincial offences officers new powers, including warrants, production orders and search powers to investigate offences
Increases fines for directors and officers convicted of offences to up to $200,000 for a first offence and $400,000 for repeat offences
Adds a right to ongoing caregiver support in the Retirement Homes Act and lets senior ministry officials direct homes on infectious disease prevention
Declares October each year as Kids' Online Safety and Privacy Month in Ontario
Aims to raise awareness about children's safety and privacy while using the Internet
Highlights risks like cyberbullying, online grooming, exploitation and trafficking facing children online
Encourages parents to be educated and equipped to supervise children's online activities
Supports discussion of online safety in schools to inform children about risks
Takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Creates 150-metre access zones around religious institutions like churches, mosques, synagogues and temples
Bans advising, persuading or persistently asking people to avoid entering a religious institution within the zone
Prohibits intimidation, physical interference, threatening conduct or repeated following within the zone
Bans repeated phone, fax or electronic communications meant to dissuade someone after they ask it to stop
Sets fines up to $5,000 or six months jail for a first offence, higher penalties for repeat offences
Allows people who suffer losses from violations to sue for damages
Lets courts issue injunctions and lets police arrest offenders without a warrant
Exempts long-term care home construction entirely from municipal development charges
Lets residential developers pay development charges at occupancy permit or first occupancy, whichever is earlier
Requires Minister's approval before municipalities amend certain official plan provisions, effective retroactively from May 12, 2025
Prevents official plans and zoning by-laws from blocking elementary or secondary schools on urban residential land
Restricts municipalities from passing by-laws about building construction or demolition timelines
Lets the Minister order municipalities and their agencies to hand over data, contracts and documents for transit and infrastructure projects
Expands which transit projects count as priority projects and eases approval requirements for transit-oriented community land deals
Authorizes up to $197,120,171,300 in public service expenses for April 1, 2024 to March 31, 2025
Authorizes up to $6,080,302,200 for public service investments in capital assets, loans and other investments
Authorizes up to $355,400,500 for expenses of Legislative Offices, including the Assembly, Auditor General and Ombudsman
Repeals the Interim Appropriation for 2024-2025 Act, 2023 and the Supplementary Interim Appropriation for 2024-2025 Act, 2024
Allows spending to be incurred by whichever ministry holds responsibility for a program during the fiscal year
Is deemed to have come into force on April 1, 2024, with the Act itself repealed starting April 1, 2026
Sets out detailed funding amounts by ministry in Schedules A, B and C
Amends the Health Protection and Promotion Act to set maximum patient-to-nurse ratios
Requires a 1-to-1 ratio for critical care patients on ventilators
Requires a 2-to-1 ratio for critical care patients not on ventilators and highly dependent mental health patients
Requires a 3-to-1 ratio for specialized care patients
Requires a 4-to-1 ratio for inpatient and palliative care patients
Requires a 5-to-1 ratio for rehabilitative care, except 7-to-1 on night shifts
Lets regulations set the required mix of nurse practitioners, registered nurses and practical nurses
Creates a new non-refundable tax credit for children's extra-curricular activities in Ontario
The credit can reduce tax owed by up to $1,000 per year
Applies to Ontario residents for taxation years ending after December 31, 2024
Cabinet may make regulations setting rules for administering the credit, including required receipts
The Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Short title is the Taxation Amendment Act (Promoting Leisure Activities for Youth), 2025
Creates the Foodbelt Protection Plan Advisory Committee with members appointed within 60 days of Royal Assent
Committee members drawn from farmers, agricultural experts, soil scientists, planners and food/agricultural organizations
Committee will recommend a Foodbelt Protection Plan to preserve a continuous agricultural land base and reduce land speculation
Committee must consult broadly with the agricultural community and publish its report within 12 months of Royal Assent
Minister of Agriculture must report to the Assembly within 60 days of receiving the Committee's report
Amends the Planning Act to block rezoning or use changes on designated agricultural land without an Agricultural Impact Assessment
This assessment requirement applies to both municipal zoning by-laws and Minister's Zoning Orders
Declares the first full week of October each year as Ontario University Athletics Week
The Act took effect immediately upon receiving Royal Assent
Official short title is the Ontario University Athletics Week Act, 2025
Requires care home landlords to itemize charges for care services and meals separately in agreements
Charges for care services and meals must match the landlord's information package and be the same for every tenant
Landlords must let tenants choose individual services from a package instead of paying for a bundle
Allows tenants and landlords to sign separate written agreements for extra care services or meals, which tenants can reduce or cancel with 10 days notice
Bans increasing care service or meal charges more than once every 12 months and caps yearly increases at the rent guideline percentage
Voids any charge increase that breaks these rules, with limited regulated exceptions capped at 3 per cent over three years
Requires retirement home operators closing down to tell residents they keep their tenant rights and that closure notice is not a termination notice
Lets Ontario's assessment corporation and tax officials send notices electronically instead of only by mail
Removes cities' and municipalities' power to create toll highways, including in Toronto
Bans automated speed and red light camera contracts that pay suppliers based on tickets issued
Requires the Minister to restore certain Toronto bicycle lanes for motor vehicle traffic on Bloor, University, Avenue Road and Yonge
Increases maximum fines for securities and commodity futures offences from $5 million to $10 million
Cuts beer basic tax rates for microbrewers and spirits tax rate from 61.5% to 30.75% starting August 1, 2025
Creates a new refundable Ontario fertility treatment tax credit equal to 25% of eligible expenses up to $20,000
Renames the Solicitor General's emergency management role to a new Minister of Emergency Preparedness and Response
Creates a Commissioner of Emergency Management and an 'Ontario Corps' to coordinate emergency personnel and resources
Requires a Cabinet advisory committee and a provincial emergency management strategy reviewed every five years
Sets rules for municipal heads of council declaring emergencies, including notifying the Minister and reporting every 30 days
Requires municipalities, ministries and critical infrastructure operators to develop emergency management plans matching a new provincial framework
Lets the Minister issue directives to community and social service agencies during extraordinary situations, with compliance orders for breaches
Creates fines up to $5,000 for individuals and $25,000 for organizations that knowingly violate a compliance order
Creates two new provincial park classes: Urban Class Parks and Adventure Class Parks
Urban Class Parks aim to improve access to nature-based recreation in or near urban centres
Adventure Class Parks support activities like rock climbing, tree-top trekking, mountain biking and off-road vehicles
Classifies Charleston Lake Provincial Park as an adventure class park
Classifies Uxbridge Urban Provincial Park as an urban class park
Allows the government to create further park classes and set their objectives by regulation
Requires adventure class park management plans to maintain existing compatible uses
Renames the Forest Fires Prevention Act to the Wildland Fire Management Act, replacing forest fire terms with wildland fire terms
Creates new categories of officers (wildland fire officer, compliance officer, investigator, enforcement officer) with search, arrest, and seizure powers
Requires municipalities and certain entities in fire regions to prepare and yearly update wildland fire management plans
Allows the Minister to declare wildland fire emergency areas and issue permits for otherwise prohibited activities
Introduces remediation orders and administrative penalties, with fines up to $50,000 for individuals and $500,000 for corporations
Enacts the Geologic Carbon Storage Act, 2025 to regulate underground carbon dioxide storage through permits and a new Carbon Storage Stewardship Fund
Amends the Surveyors Act to allow limited and temporary licences and lets applicants appeal certain committee decisions
Creates the Homelessness Ends with Housing Act, 2025 to guide efforts to end homelessness
Requires the Ontario government to design a strategy aiming to eliminate homelessness within 10 years
Sets strategy goals like better data collection, more deeply affordable rental units and supportive housing
Calls for increased funding to the Canada-Ontario Housing Benefit and a housing-first approach
Requires the Minister to create an 11-member Homelessness Advisory Committee within 90 days, including people who experienced homelessness
Requires an annual public report tracking numbers of unhoused people, deaths, repeat homelessness and available units
Allows the Lieutenant Governor in Council to prescribe extra information for future reports
Declares the first week of June each year as Extreme Heat Awareness Week in Ontario
Requires the Minister of the Environment, Conservation and Parks to publish extreme heat information on a government website
Website must cover preparation, prevention, health risks, resources and FAQs about extreme heat
Minister must mail this extreme heat information yearly to households in territories without municipal organization
Amends the City of Toronto Act to require extreme heat information be sent with tax bills
Amends the Municipal Act to require municipal treasurers to include extreme heat information with tax bills
Most requirements take effect three months after the Act receives Royal Assent
Requires job posting platforms to let users report fraudulent job ads and to post a written policy on handling them
Gives workers three days unpaid leave to search for jobs after receiving termination notice, when 50 or more employees are laid off
Allows employers and employees to agree to extended layoffs of 35 or more weeks (up to 78 weeks) with Director approval, avoiding termination pay
Lets Ontario limit municipal and Toronto zoning powers over buildings funded for training or skills development, exempting them from some Planning Act rules
Requires reimbursement of defibrillator costs to employers required to install them under workplace safety rules
Creates a new administrative penalty system letting workplace safety inspectors fine employers for violations without going to court
Increases workplace insurance penalties, allowing fines up to $750,000 per conviction for repeated offences and adding rules against false claims statements
Amends the Marriage Act to let members of the Legislative Assembly solemnize marriages under a licence
Members must give written notice to the Minister to gain this authority
The authority continues for 12 months after the person stops being a member of the Assembly
The Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Amends the Resource Recovery and Circular Economy Act, 2016 to create a beverage container deposit program
Requires a deposit of at least 10 cents for containers one litre or less, 25 cents for larger containers
Defines 'grocery store' based on size, food product variety, and floor space rules
Requires grocery stores and Brewers Retail Inc. stores to act as collection depots for beverage containers
Requires these stores to refund the deposit to people returning beverage containers
Makes it an offence for Brewers Retail Inc. or grocery store owners to fail to comply with the collection depot and refund rules
Comes into force one year after receiving Royal Assent
Requires children's aid societies and licensees to inform children, young persons and others about the Ombudsman, in language suited to their understanding
Requires children's aid societies to review and update their by-laws and make them public, per Minister's rules
Requires Minister's approval before societies enter certain financial transactions affecting their budget
Removes maternity homes from exclusion in the definition of 'institution' under child welfare law
Lets the Minister investigate school boards over public interest concerns and direct boards to take action
Allows the Minister to take control of a school board's administration if directions are not followed
Requires colleges and universities to admit students based on merit, publish admission criteria, and develop research security plans
Removes the cap that limited MPP annual salaries to the 2009 level
Sets the Government House Leader's salary addition at 19.2 per cent
Ends membership in the old MPP pension plan for current members, effective 2026
Makes MPPs members of the Public Service Pension Plan instead, with special vesting rules for the 44th Parliament
Allows the government to create a new MPP supplemental pension plan by order, with terms set out in a schedule
Requires Board of Internal Economy consent before benefits or contribution rates in the supplemental plan can change
Lets MPPs choose how to transfer or use funds from their old pension account, with a statement due by February 1, 2026
Requires a licence to establish, operate or maintain a zoo in Ontario
Sets out application requirements including animal inventories, site plans and emergency plans
Lets the Registrar issue, refuse, suspend or revoke licences based on set conditions and grounds
Gives licensees the right to a hearing before the Director if a licence is refused, suspended or revoked
Requires annual inspections of zoos and allows inspectors to order fixes for violations
Allows removal of animals from unlicensed zoos and sets fines up to $50,000 for individuals and $250,000 for corporations
Gives existing zoo operators one year to get licensed and lets some current wild animal owners keep animals until they die
Adds a new Part IV.1 to the Occupational Health and Safety Act to address heat stress at work
Requires the Minister to create a Worker Heat Protection Standard within 12 months of the section coming into force
Standard must include engineering controls, work schedule adjustments, breaks and employer-paid protective equipment
Employers must create a Heat Stress and Protection Policy, do heat stress assessments, and review annually
Workers must have access to cool drinking water near work areas and get heat stress training
Employees must be paid their regular wage for rest breaks, medical removal and training time under the standard
Minister must report yearly to the Legislature on heat-related illness, deaths and enforcement for five years
Declares the fourth week in March each year as Flooding Awareness Week
Requires the Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing to publish flood preparedness and prevention information on a government website
Requires a guide to flooding resources and FAQs about flooding risks in Ontario to be published online
Requires the Minister to mail flooding information yearly to households in territories without municipal organization
Requires Toronto's city treasurer to send flooding information along with tax bills to taxpayers
Requires municipal treasurers under the Municipal Act to send flooding information along with tax bills
Most provisions take effect three months after the Act receives Royal Assent
Proclaims September of each year as Ethiopian Heritage Month in Ontario
Recognizes contributions of Ethiopian Canadians to Ontario's social, economic and cultural life
References cultural events like Enkutatash, Maskel and Irreechaa celebrated in September
Act took effect immediately upon receiving Royal Assent
Short title given is the Ethiopian Heritage Month Act, 2025
Restricts when Ontario bills can use the notwithstanding clause under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
Allows its use only for urgent, temporary situations seriously endangering Ontarians' lives, health or safety
Also allows its use to amend a law a court found violated the Charter, limited to the specific provisions found in contravention
Requires the Attorney General to table a report justifying the clause's use within 30 days of the bill's introduction
Report must explain why alternatives to using the clause were considered inadequate
Requires a two-thirds majority vote of elected members to pass any bill invoking the notwithstanding clause
Allows regulations to require data centres and other large electricity users to meet specific conditions before connecting to the grid
Adds economic growth and hydrogen market development as new goals for Ontario's electricity system
Lets the government pay transmitters or cover certain electricity costs directly from public funds instead of through consumer rates
Removes the requirement for municipal voters to approve by-laws granting public utility rights on municipal highways
Expands Ontario Energy Board's power to approve construction, extension or addition of gas distribution works, not just operation
Lets utilities create special accounts to track costs from complying with rules restricting procurement based on country of origin, if Bill 5 passes
Gives the Ontario Energy Board's CEO authority to set internal policies on hearing timelines and information requirements
Creates the 9-1-1 Everywhere in Ontario Act, 2025 to improve emergency call services across the province
Requires the Minister to ensure everyone dialing 9-1-1 connects to a call centre or local police service
Sets a December 2026 deadline for compatible computer dispatch systems allowing information sharing and caller location tracking
Requires an interoperable radio channel for multi-agency responses among health, police, ambulance and fire services
Requires call centres to have adequate staffing, trained supervisors, mental health supports and direct communication between responders
Mandates a written policy covering communication with callers, accountability for delays, and mandatory reviews after deaths
Amends the Ombudsman Act to create an Assistant Ombudsman overseeing 9-1-1 operations and public awareness campaigns
Enacts the Justice for Soli Act (Stop Criminalizing Mental Health), 2025
Requires the Ontario government to recognize correctional facilities are not appropriate for people in mental health crises
States mental illness requires health care and should not be criminalized
References the inquest into the death of Soleiman (Soli) Faqiri, ruled a homicide
Aligns with the first of 57 recommendations from the Chief Coroner's inquest report
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Declares the week starting on the third Monday of September each year as Consent Awareness Week in Ontario
Aims to promote public understanding and practice of consent
Cites that only 45 per cent of Canadians fully understand what consent entails
References 2019 data showing about 940,000 sexual assault incidents, with only 6 per cent reported to police
Notes 45 colleges and universities already hold Consent Awareness Week activities on campus
Encourages all post-secondary institutions and Ontarians to mark the week with awareness activities
Act takes effect immediately upon receiving Royal Assent
Requires hospitals and long-term care homes in municipalities of 8,000 or more to create plans limiting spending on staffing agencies
Sets timelines to phase out staffing agency use over 24 months, with limits varying by municipality size
Requires new healthcare staffing agencies to operate as not-for-profits
Subjects agencies receiving over $400,000 from government to oversight by Auditor General, Ombudsman, Patient Ombudsman and Integrity Commissioner
Caps agency worker pay at no more than 10 per cent above the existing rate for that profession
Bans agencies from poaching employees from hospitals or long-term care homes, with fines up to $1,000,000
Prohibits agencies from assigning workers to the same or adjacent Ontario Health Team they recently left
Allows the Minister to appoint up to six Deputy Provincial Land and Development Facilitators, up from four
Transfers jurisdiction over highways and bridges from Peel Region to Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon by July 1, 2026 or a date set by the Minister
Transfers jurisdiction over waste collection from Peel Region to Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon by January 1, 2026 or a date set by the Minister
Bars Peel Region from passing a by-law to reclaim waste collection powers from these cities until December 31, 2035
Gives the Minister broad regulation-making power to manage the transfer of assets, staff, contracts and finances between Peel and the three municipalities
Shields the Crown, Peel Region, Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon from lawsuits or damages related to this jurisdiction transfer, even for past actions
Blocks most court, administrative or arbitration claims tied to the transfer, except judicial review or constitutional claims
Requires municipalities and Toronto to post audited financial statements online instead of publishing them in newspapers, within 60 days
Allows sex offender registry information to be shared with prescribed entities for crime prevention or law enforcement, under a required agreement
Rewrites consumer protection rules on rewards points, letting government set new rules on expiry, disclosure and even apply them to past agreements
Removes email addresses from information consumer reporting agencies must disclose about who accessed a person's credit file
Permits open liquor consumption in designated public areas of operating provincial parks
Lets funeral operators be required to get authorization before providing certain services on human remains, with court power to decide who holds that authority
Changes Royal Ontario Museum's board size to 13-21 trustees, with 7-15 appointed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council instead of a fixed 15
Amends the Highway Traffic Act to create penalties for offences causing death or serious bodily harm
Applies when a person commits an offence and causes or contributes to an accident causing death or serious injury
Sets a fine of not less than $2,000 and not more than $50,000 on conviction
Allows imprisonment for a term of not more than two years, or both fine and imprisonment
Permits suspension of the person's driver's licence or permit for up to five years
Comes into force on the day it receives Royal Assent
Transfers control of Ottawa Road 174 and County Road 17 from a municipality to the Ministry of Transportation
These highways will no longer count as part of any municipality's road system
Existing agreements or permits about the highways continue as if made by the Minister instead
Rights and benefits municipalities had under those agreements now belong to the Crown in right of Ontario
Blocks the Lieutenant Governor in Council from ordering these highways to be transferred back to a municipality
The change takes effect on the day the bill receives Royal Assent
The short title is the Uploading Highways 174 and 17 Act, 2025
Requires scales and inspection sites on Highway 11 north of North Bay and Highway 17 to be staffed at least 12 hours daily
Requires the government to ensure OPP traffic enforcement staffing is sufficient to enforce the Highway Traffic Act
Requires commercial truck drivers to be tested by a Ministry-certified examiner before getting a driver education certificate
Puts the Ministry of Transportation in charge of managing winter maintenance on Highway 11 north of North Bay and Highway 17
Allows the Ministry to work with contractors and providers for winter highway maintenance
Act takes effect on the day it receives Royal Assent
Lets municipalities and local boards charge fees to gas producers, distributors, transmitters and storage companies
Fees can apply for services, activities, costs payable or use of property on municipal highways
Applies to wires, cables, poles, conduits, pipes, equipment, machinery or other works used in the gas business
Blocks provincial regulations from limiting this municipal fee-charging power
Makes matching changes to both the Municipal Act, 2001 and the City of Toronto Act, 2006
Comes into force immediately upon receiving Royal Assent
Short title is the No Free Ride for Fossil Fuels Act, 2025
Requires landlords to keep rental properties in good repair regardless of any effort made to do so
Lets tenants apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board when a landlord ignores a mediated settlement or prior repair order
Allows fines up to $1,000 per day or rent abatements for landlords who fail to complete ordered repairs
Sets new rules capping rent charged to a new tenant based on the previous tenant's lawful rent
Creates a public rent registry requiring landlords to file rent and address information within 30 days of a new lease
Bars landlords from raising rent if they have not filed the required registry statement
Requires free mandatory legal representation for tenants facing above-guideline rent increase applications
Amends the Building Code Act, 1992 to require new houses to be built EV-charger ready
Applies to new houses under Part 9 of the building code with a garage, carport or driveway
Requires builders to install a minimum 200 amp panel board in these homes
Requires a conduit of at least 27 mm trade size with a means to pull cables through
Requires a square 4-11/16 inch electrical outlet box near the garage, carport or driveway
Conduit and outlet box must block gas and exhaust fumes from passing through
Rules apply only to houses built after the section comes into force
Requires new or renovated correctional institutions to have at least 20 percent of inmate beds in mental health support units
Prohibits cruel, inhumane or degrading treatment or punishment of inmates
Bans overly rigorous physical restraints, excessive surveillance, sensory deprivation and disorientation of inmates
Prohibits withholding food, exercise, human contact or medical care as punishment
Requires superintendents to ensure treatment complies with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
Bans segregation, defined as highly restricted movement and association for 22 or more hours a day
Creates an Independent Review Panel to review cases of inmates held in restrictive confinement
Reverses 2015 changes to the Government Advertising Act, restoring earlier Auditor General review rules
Bans government offices from publishing, displaying or broadcasting ads before Auditor General review results are received
Requires ads to state they are paid for by the Government of Ontario
Bans use of Executive Council or Assembly members' names, voices or images in government ads, with exceptions for ads targeted outside Ontario
Bans partisan advertising or ads primarily meant to boost the governing party's image or attack critics
Restricts government ads during election writ periods, with exceptions for revenue-generating or time-sensitive items
Renames the law the End the Public Funding of Partisan Government Advertising Act, 2025
Requires the Ontario government to formally recognize intimate partner violence as an epidemic in the province
Directs the Attorney General to create a Renfrew County Inquest Implementation Committee within 30 days of the section taking effect
Committee membership must equally split between senior ministry officials and community experts on intimate partner violence
One community expert member must chair the Committee
Committee will review the 86 recommendations from the 2022 Renfrew County triple femicide inquest and plan implementation steps
Committee must publish a first report within 12 months, then updates every 12 months, tabled in the Legislature and posted online
Lieutenant Governor in Council may set remuneration and expenses for members, subject to funds being appropriated by the Legislature
Sets new rules limiting what water protection plans can require for activities identified as significant drinking water threats
Lets forest management plans cover multiple management units and removes annual harvest approval requirement
Expands who can perform pharmacy-related tasks by allowing additional prescribed persons beyond College members
Lets the Minister order municipalities to install school zone signs, doing it themselves if municipality refuses
Repeals automated speed enforcement system rules and blocks lawsuits against government over ended camera contracts
Creates faster registration process for out-of-province health professionals applying to certain Colleges, with 2-business-day decisions
Renames the Species at Risk framework, updating definitions and habitat protection order rules under new Species Conservation Act
Vacates the seat of the Haldimand County trustee on the Brant Haldimand Norfolk Catholic District School Board
The trustee traveled to Europe with three others in July 2024 using Board-reimbursed public funds
This trustee refused to repay $12,370 in expenses, unlike three colleagues who repaid in full
Bars this trustee from running for any school board office in the next regular election
Bans this trustee from being appointed or running in any school board by-election until November 14, 2030
Blocks lawsuits or claims for damages against the Crown, the school board, or Haldimand County over this law
Allows only judicial review or constitutional remedy claims, not other compensation claims
